..(Thursday night through Tuesday)
Issued at 444 AM EST WED NOV 18 2026

At the start of the long term period, midlevel ridging will be 
centered over the Midwest, with a shortwave trough over the 
forecast area. Meanwhile, farther west, deep troughing associated 
with a closed upper level low will be centered over the Pacific 
Coast. With time, the initial shortwave will translate eastward, 
allowing for ridging to briefly build back into the forecast area,
with modest 500 mb height rises during the day on Friday. 
Initially, this ridging will maintain quiet weather; however, by 
the end of the weekend, the eastward progression of the 
aforementioned trough will mark a shift towards more active 
weather.

At the surface, high pressure will be located just east of the 
forecast area initially. However, as ridging shifts eastward and 
the shortwave progresses along the ridge periphery, the surface 
high will lift to the northeast, with local winds becoming more 
southeasterly with time. Despite this downslope orientation, a 
weak pressure gradient will keep winds light enough to mute drying
effects somewhat, although the air mass in place will still 
remain dry. High temperatures will be above average on Friday and 
Saturday, rising into the upper 60s and low 70s, with clear to 
mostly clear skies and light winds supporting moderate 
ridge/valley splits on Thursday and Friday nights, accompanied by 
patchy fog in typical river valleys. By Saturday, flow aloft will 
become more southwesterly, which will allow for total atmospheric 
moisture to increase, with LREF mean PW values climbing to 0.7" or
higher, representing at least the 75th percentile compared to 
climatology. Combined with the approaching system, this moisture 
will allow for cloud cover to begin to increase later on Saturday,
which will likely keep lows milder than in previous days, 
although a slower increase in cloud cover could allow for one more
night of defined ridge/valley splits with cooler than expected 
lows in valley locales.

As the associated surface low translates eastward across the 
Ontario/Great Lakes region, a cold front will approach the 
Commonwealth by early Sunday. This will bring the first 
mentionable PoPs to eastern Kentucky in nearly a week. However, 
QPF with this frontal passage will likely be meager. The forecast 
area will be well displaced from the surface low, mitigating 
moisture return before the frontal passage, particularly given the
aforementioned antecedent downslope winds. Additionally, 
deterministic guidance is in fairly good agreement that, at the 
same time, a deep coastal low will be pushing northward into the 
Carolinas. In this setup, eastern Kentucky will be caught between 
flow around this feature and the Canadian low, introducing 
additional uncertainty regarding the nature of moisture advection 
ahead of the front. In fact, some recent individual deterministic 
model runs are even hinting that precipitation associated with the
Carolina low may graze far eastern Kentucky. In short, there is 
still significant uncertainty regarding how these features 
interact. This can be seen in disagreements regarding just how dry
the air mass will be going into this frontal passage, with LREF 
dewpoints demonstrating a whopping 11 degree difference between 
25th and 75th percentile dewpoints early on Sunday morning. 
However, even given these discrepancies, the most recent ensemble 
guidance suggests that it is very likely (80-90% chance) that the 
forecast area will receive some measurable rain this weekend into 
early Monday (with some deterministic guidance delaying the 
frontal passage until Monday). Thus, although forecast details 
remain uncertain at this time, confidence in rainfall on 
Sunday/Monday is increasing. Behind the front, a cooler pattern 
will set in, with CAA via northwesterly winds keeping temperatures
slightly below average on Monday and Tuesday. Any additional 
precipitation looks to hold off until at least midweek.
